claims.claim: Dynamic and extended lactation periods evolved in marsupials as an alternative to the complex placentation seen in eutherians.
claims.source: As marsupial milk is clearly supplied to support fetal development, a role fulfilled primarily by the placenta in eutherians, it has been proposed that dynamic and extended lactation periods evolved in marsupials as an alternative to the complex placentation seen in eutherians (Renfree, 1983; Tyndale-Biscoe and Renfree, 1987; Renfree, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Renfree, 1983; Tyndale-Biscoe and Renfree, 1987; Renfree, 2010.

claims.claim: 445 transcripts were differentially expressed between BOM and TOM tissues.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 445 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 83 were up-regulated in BOM tissue and 362 were up-regulated in TOM tissue (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: 83 transcripts were up-regulated in BOM tissue compared to TOM.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 445 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 83 were up-regulated in BOM tissue and 362 were up-regulated in TOM tissue (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: 362 transcripts were up-regulated in TOM tissue compared to BOM.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 445 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 83 were up-regulated in BOM tissue and 362 were up-regulated in TOM tissue (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: BOM up-regulated genes are associated with ontology related to endocytosis and metabolism.
claims.source: The BOM up-regulated genes are associated with ontology related to endocytosis and metabolism (p-adj = 0.0764, 0.0390, see Supplementary file 1) consistent with the hypothesis that BOM acts as the center for embryonic nutrient uptake (Renfree, 1973b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: BOM acts as the center for embryonic nutrient uptake.
claims.source: The BOM up-regulated genes are associated with ontology related to endocytosis and metabolism (p-adj = 0.0764, 0.0390, see Supplementary file 1) consistent with the hypothesis that BOM acts as the center for embryonic nutrient uptake (Renfree, 1973b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology data and a citation to Renfree, 1973b.

claims.claim: TOM up-regulated genes are associated with ontology related to extracellular matrix organization, hematopoiesis, and response to oxygen levels.
claims.source: Conversely, the genes up-regulated in TOM are associated with ontology related to extracellular matrix organization, hematopoiesis, and response to oxygen levels (p-adj = 1.49×10−7, 0.00193, 0.0688, see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: TOM acts as the center of embryonic respiration.
claims.source: This is consistent with the idea that TOM, being the vascularized component of the tammar placenta, acts as the center of embryonic respiration (Renfree, 1973b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology data and a citation to Renfree, 1973b.

claims.claim: BOM and TOM have specific and distinct functions throughout gestation.
claims.source: Overall, this supports the suggestion that BOM and TOM have specific and distinct functions throughout gestation (Renfree, 1973b) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previously observed morphology differences (Freyer et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the differential expression data, citations, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: TOM begins to expand through day 23 of gestation until it has covered 50% of the yolk sac.
claims.source: After the shell coat is lost by gestational day 18, TOM begins to expand through day 23 of gestation until it has covered 50% of the yolk sac (Freyer et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Freyer et al., 2002.

claims.claim: 1705 transcripts were differentially expressed between early (day 21-23) and late (day 25) placental time points.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 1705 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 592 were up-regulated at day 21–23 (early) and 1113 were up-regulated at day 25 (late) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 592 transcripts were up-regulated at day 21-23 (early) compared to day 25.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 1705 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 592 were up-regulated at day 21–23 (early) and 1113 were up-regulated at day 25 (late) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 1113 transcripts were up-regulated at day 25 (late) compared to day 21-23.
claims.source: Using DESeq2, we find 1705 differentially expressed transcripts; of which 592 were up-regulated at day 21–23 (early) and 1113 were up-regulated at day 25 (late) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the DESeq2 analysis and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Genes up-regulated at earlier time points trended toward intracellular and ion transport.
claims.source: Genes up-regulated at earlier time points exhibited no significant enrichment for any gene ontology, but trended toward intracellular and ion transport (p-adj = 0.188, 0.109, see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: Genes up-regulated at later time points were enriched for cellular growth, differentiation, and junction organization.
claims.source: In contrast, those up-regulated at later time points were enriched for cellular growth, differentiation, and junction organization (p-adj = 0.0331, 0.0162, 5.79 × 10−4, see Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: The tammar placenta undergoes dynamic changes in gene expression throughout its development despite the short duration of its physiological activity.
claims.source: Overall, these findings reveal that the tammar placenta undergoes dynamic changes in gene expression throughout its development despite the short duration of its physiological activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal differential expression data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: 3894 transcripts are shared by tammar, mouse, and human placentas.
claims.source: We found 3894 transcripts shared by all three species (Supplementary file 2) which included many factors that have documented roles in placental function (Rawn and Cross, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis.

claims.claim: The tammar placenta expresses trophoblast markers including Gcm1, members of the Igf signaling pathway, placental cytokeratins, Wnt7b, Stra13, PTN, and Gjb3.
claims.source: We uncovered the expression of trophoblast markers including: Gcm1 (Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000), members of the Igf signaling pathway (Reik et al., 2003), many placental cytokeratins (Gauster et al., 2013), Wnt7b (Parr et al., 2001), Stra13 (Hughes et al., 2004), PTN (Schulte et al., 1996), and Gjb3 (Koch et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data and citations for each marker.

claims.claim: The tammar placenta expresses cathepsins and serpins, which are important for mediating maternal fetal interactions.
claims.source: Cathepsins (Mason, 2008) and Serpins (Kaiserman et al., 2002) a class of proteases and protease inhibitors respectively, which are important for mediating maternal fetal interactions were also present (Hannibal and Baker, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data and citations.

claims.claim: The tammar placenta expresses markers of the maternal decidua such as Cebpb and Vim.
claims.source: We also found markers of the maternal decidua such as Cebpb (Lynch et al., 2011) and Vim (Can et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data and citations.

claims.claim: The tammar and mouse placentas share the expression of Cdx2, a transcription factor essential for early trophoblast development.
claims.source: Additionally, the tammar and mouse placentas share the expression of Cdx2, a transcription factor that is essential for early trophoblast development (Strumpf et al., 2005; Frankenberg et al., 2013), while the tammar and human placentas share expression of Nodal, a secreted factor important for trophoblast differentiation (Ma et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data and citations to Strumpf et al., 2005 and Frankenberg et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The tammar and human placentas share expression of Nodal, a secreted factor important for trophoblast differentiation.
claims.source: Additionally, the tammar and mouse placentas share the expression of Cdx2, a transcription factor that is essential for early trophoblast development (Strumpf et al., 2005; Frankenberg et al., 2013), while the tammar and human placentas share expression of Nodal, a secreted factor important for trophoblast differentiation (Ma et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data and a citation to Ma et al., 2001.

claims.claim: A core set of genes is essential for placental function and development across all therian mammals.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with the idea that a core set of genes is essential for placental function and development across all therian mammals and that, regardless of morphological differences, both marsupial and eutherian placentas share expression of key placental transcripts.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative transcriptome data showing shared gene expression.

claims.claim: The eutherian placenta is derived from both fetal trophoblast and maternal decidua cells.
claims.source: Eutherian and marsupial placentas have key differences in their cellular composition: the eutherian placenta is derived from both fetal trophoblast and maternal decidua cells, and the marsupial placenta is derived solely from fetal trophoblast and yolk sac endoderm cells.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about eutherian placental biology.

claims.claim: The marsupial placenta is derived solely from fetal trophoblast and yolk sac endoderm cells.
claims.source: Eutherian and marsupial placentas have key differences in their cellular composition: the eutherian placenta is derived from both fetal trophoblast and maternal decidua cells, and the marsupial placenta is derived solely from fetal trophoblast and yolk sac endoderm cells.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about marsupial placental biology.

claims.claim: CDX2, CEBPB and Vimentin are expressed in both the endodermal and trophoblast layers of the tammar placenta.
claims.source: We find that CDX2, CEBPB and Vimentin are expressed in both the endodermal and trophoblast layers, with CDX2 and CEPBP being nuclear and Vimentin cytoplasmic.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CDX2 and CEBPB are nuclear proteins in the tammar placenta.
claims.source: We find that CDX2, CEBPB and Vimentin are expressed in both the endodermal and trophoblast layers, with CDX2 and CEPBP being nuclear and Vimentin cytoplasmic.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Vimentin is a cytoplasmic protein in the tammar placenta.
claims.source: We find that CDX2, CEBPB and Vimentin are expressed in both the endodermal and trophoblast layers, with CDX2 and CEPBP being nuclear and Vimentin cytoplasmic.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CEBPB and Vimentin are known markers of maternal decidua in eutherians.
claims.source: This is particularly intriguing as CEBPB (Lynch et al., 2011) and Vimentin (Can et al., 1995) are known markers of maternal decidua in eutherians and have limited expression in the eutherian trophoblast.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lynch et al., 2011 and Can et al., 1995.

claims.claim: CEBPB and Vimentin have limited expression in the eutherian trophoblast.
claims.source: This is particularly intriguing as CEBPB (Lynch et al., 2011) and Vimentin (Can et al., 1995) are known markers of maternal decidua in eutherians and have limited expression in the eutherian trophoblast.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lynch et al., 2011 and Can et al., 1995.

claims.claim: Pan-Cytokeratins and GCM1 are strongly expressed only in the endodermal layer of the tammar placenta, and are not expressed in the trophoblast layer.
claims.source: Additionally, we find that the known eutherian markers for trophoblasts, Pan-Cytokeratins (Gauster et al., 2013) and GCM1(Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000) are strongly expressed only in the endodermal layer, and are not expressed in the trophoblast layer.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3 and citations.

claims.claim: The choriovitelline placenta in tammar has accomplished coordination of critical placental functions and may include functions that are supplied maternally in eutherians.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that the choriovitelline placenta in tammar has accomplished coordination of critical placental functions and may even include functions that are supplied maternally in eutherians.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the protein localization data showing expression of both maternal and fetal markers.

claims.claim: The mouse and human placenta are molecularly distinct between the first half and second half of pregnancy.
claims.source: While we demonstrate that the tammar placental transcriptome shares molecular similarities to the term eutherian placenta, the mouse and human placenta are molecularly distinct between the first half and second half of pregnancy, with the early stages primarily involved in cell cycle and metabolism and the later stages focused on reproduction (Knox and Baker, 2008; Winn et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knox and Baker, 2008 and Winn et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Early stages of mouse and human placentation are primarily involved in cell cycle and metabolism.
claims.source: While we demonstrate that the tammar placental transcriptome shares molecular similarities to the term eutherian placenta, the mouse and human placenta are molecularly distinct between the first half and second half of pregnancy, with the early stages primarily involved in cell cycle and metabolism and the later stages focused on reproduction (Knox and Baker, 2008; Winn et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knox and Baker, 2008 and Winn et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Later stages of mouse and human placentation are focused on reproduction.
claims.source: While we demonstrate that the tammar placental transcriptome shares molecular similarities to the term eutherian placenta, the mouse and human placenta are molecularly distinct between the first half and second half of pregnancy, with the early stages primarily involved in cell cycle and metabolism and the later stages focused on reproduction (Knox and Baker, 2008; Winn et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knox and Baker, 2008 and Winn et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The transcriptome of the tammar placenta, regardless of gestational age, is more similar to that of an e10.5 mouse placenta than any other time point.
claims.source: The highest coefficients reveal that the transcriptome of the tammar placenta, regardless of gestational age, is more similar to that of an e10.5 mouse placenta than any other time point (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The mouse placenta has higher correlations at all time points with the tammar placenta than it does with the mouse heart.
claims.source: Finally, we find that the mouse placenta has higher correlations at all time points with the tammar placenta than it does with the mouse heart (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 410 transcripts are unique to the mouse placenta, with 340 expressed prior to e12.5 and 70 expressed after e12.5.
claims.source: In a previous study, we identified 410 transcripts are unique to the mouse placenta (Knox and Baker, 2008). During gestation 340 of these transcripts are expressed prior to e12.5 and 70 are expressed after e12.5 of mouse gestation, demarcating an early and late placental signature (Knox and Baker, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knox and Baker, 2008.

claims.claim: 100 tammar orthologs of the 410 mouse placental transcripts are expressed in the tammar placenta at days 21, 23 and 25 gestation.
claims.source: We found 100 tammar orthologs of these 410 mouse placental transcripts expressed in our datasets at 21, 23 and 25 days gestation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis.

claims.claim: Of the 100 tammar orthologs, 90 are expressed only in the early mouse placenta and 10 are expressed only in the late mouse placenta.
claims.source: Of these 100, 90 are expressed only in the early mouse placenta (prior to 12.5) and 10 are expressed only in the late mouse placenta (after 12.5) (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: There is a significant enrichment of early placental transcripts in the tammar placenta compared to late placental transcripts.
claims.source: When comparing the early transcripts (90/340) to the late placental transcripts (10/70), we find a significant enrichment of early transcripts (p<0.05 by chi-square test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test).

claims.claim: Tammar placentation functionally resembles the earlier phases of mouse placentation.
claims.source: Overall, this more targeted analysis supports the idea that tammar placentation functionally resembles the earlier phases of mouse placentation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment analysis of early vs late placental transcripts.

claims.claim: Igf2 was imprinted in the tammar mammary gland.
claims.source: Previously, it was demonstrated that Igf2 was imprinted in the tammar mammary gland (Stringer et al., 2012, 2014), a phenomenon previously determined to be essential for proper growth and development of the eutherian placenta (Reik et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stringer et al., 2012, 2014.

claims.claim: Igf2 imprinting is essential for proper growth and development of the eutherian placenta.
claims.source: Previously, it was demonstrated that Igf2 was imprinted in the tammar mammary gland (Stringer et al., 2012, 2014), a phenomenon previously determined to be essential for proper growth and development of the eutherian placenta (Reik et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reik et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The tammar and mouse placenta share the highest correlation of any cross-species organ pair.
claims.source: First, we find that the tammar and mouse placenta share the highest correlation of any cross-species organ pair (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), confirming the high degree of molecular similarity between the eutherian and tammar placenta that we found using immunofluorescence (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The tammar mammary gland shows the highest correlation with the mouse mammary gland when compared to any other mouse tissue.
claims.source: Second, although less so than the placenta, the tammar mammary gland shows the highest correlation with the mouse mammary gland when compared to any other mouse tissue, highlighting some functional conservation in this organ.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Gata3 and Msh2 are transcription factors known to be essential for placentation in mice.
claims.source: Among those genes with conserved expression in mammary glands, we found Gata3 (Chiu and Chen, 2016) and Msh2 (Tanaka et al., 1997), transcription factors known to be essential for placentation in mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiu and Chen, 2016 and Tanaka et al., 1997.

claims.claim: GATA3 is expressed in the alveoli of the tammar mammary gland at day 60 of lactation.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence in tammar mammary gland at day 60 of lactation finds GATA3 in the alveoli (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GATA3 expression pattern in tammar mammary gland is reminiscent of GATA3 expression in the mouse mammary gland.
claims.source: This pattern of expression is reminiscent of GATA3 expression in the mouse mammary gland (Tlsty, 2007), suggesting an ancestral role of GATA3 in mediating lactation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and a citation to Tlsty, 2007.

claims.claim: GATA3 has an ancestral role in mediating lactation.
claims.source: This pattern of expression is reminiscent of GATA3 expression in the mouse mammary gland (Tlsty, 2007), suggesting an ancestral role of GATA3 in mediating lactation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the conserved expression pattern of GATA3 in tammar and mouse mammary glands.

claims.claim: The placentas of both tammar and mouse show the lowest within species correlation with mammary gland.
claims.source: Finally, the placentas of both tammar and mouse show the lowest within species correlation with mammary gland which suggests widely divergent roles for each organ in supporting reproductive physiology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis.

claims.claim: 77 genes are shared between tammar placenta, eutherian placenta, and tammar mammary gland, but not in the mouse mammary gland.
claims.source: To this end, we identified transcripts present in eutherian placenta (Supplementary file 1), tammar placenta, tammar mammary gland, but not in the mouse mammary gland (GSE60450), finding 77 genes expressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The 77 genes shared between tammar placenta, eutherian placenta, and tammar mammary gland are associated with nutrient transport.
claims.source: The 77 genes shared between the tammar placenta, eutherian placenta, and tammar mammary gland (Figure 5A), are associated with nutrient transport (GO analysis; p-adj = 0.0163, see Supplementary file 3) and include the placental transcription factor Gcm1, which is necessary for eutherian placentation (Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: Gcm1 is necessary for eutherian placentation.
claims.source: The 77 genes shared between the tammar placenta, eutherian placenta, and tammar mammary gland (Figure 5A), are associated with nutrient transport (GO analysis; p-adj = 0.0163, see Supplementary file 3) and include the placental transcription factor Gcm1, which is necessary for eutherian placentation (Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000.

claims.claim: GCM1 shows strong nuclear staining throughout the tammar mammary gland at day 60 of lactation.
claims.source: Localization of GCM1 by immunofluorescence demonstrates strong nuclear staining throughout the tammar mammary gland at day 60 of lactation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: GCM1 is highly expressed in the alveoli of the tammar mammary gland.
claims.source: Additionally, we find high expression of GCM1 in the alveoli (Figure 5B), the site of milk ejection in the tammar mammary gland (Findlay, 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Findlay, 1982.

claims.claim: The alveoli are the site of milk ejection in the tammar mammary gland.
claims.source: Additionally, we find high expression of GCM1 in the alveoli (Figure 5B), the site of milk ejection in the tammar mammary gland (Findlay, 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Findlay, 1982.

claims.claim: GCM1 has a novel function in supporting multi-stage lactation in marsupials.
claims.source: This expression suggests a novel function of GCM1 in supporting multi-stage lactation in marsupials.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression of GCM1 in the tammar mammary gland, particularly in the alveoli.

claims.claim: 77 transcripts, including Gcm1, represent genes that have been convergently co-opted by the marsupial mammary gland to expand its potential for fetal support or lost in the eutherian mammary gland.
claims.source: Therefore, we suggest that these 77 transcripts, including Gcm1, represent genes that have been convergently co-opted by the marsupial mammary gland to expand its potential for fetal support or lost in the eutherian mammary gland where the placenta provides all the required support for fetal development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparative transcriptome analysis showing these genes are present in tammar mammary gland but not mouse mammary gland.

claims.claim: 108 transcripts are expressed in the eutherian placenta and the tammar mammary gland, but not in the tammar placenta and mouse mammary gland.
claims.source: To this end, we identified 108 transcripts that were expressed in the eutherian placenta and the tammar mammary gland, but not in the tammar placenta and mouse mammary gland (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The 108 genes shared between eutherian placenta and tammar mammary gland trended toward processes critical for reproductive success including embryonic morphogenesis and immune function.
claims.source: GO analysis of these 108 genes did not unveil significant ontology, but trended toward processes critical for reproductive success including: embryonic morphogenesis and immune function (p-adj = 0.163, 0.146, see Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis with statistical values provided.

claims.claim: Dkk1 and Csf1r have documented roles in placentation.
claims.source: Among the genes associated with these two GO terms we find Dkk1 and Csf1r, transcripts with documented roles in placentation (Pollheimer et al., 2006; Sasmono et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollheimer et al., 2006 and Sasmono et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Igfbp1 is important for regulating insulin growth factor function, a process important in both therian placentation and marsupial lactation.
claims.source: Here we also find the expression of Igfbp1, a molecule important for regulating insulin growth factor function, a process previously demonstrated to be important in both therian placentation (Reik et al., 2003) and marsupial lactation (Stringer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reik et al., 2003 and Stringer et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The tammar mammary gland performs some similar functions to the late eutherian placenta to support continued fetal development in the pouch.
claims.source: Together, these data provide molecular evidence that the tammar mammary gland performs some similar functions to the late eutherian placenta to support continued fetal development in the pouch.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative transcriptome analysis showing shared genes between eutherian placenta and tammar mammary gland.

claims.claim: The tammar yolk sac placenta performs functions that the eutherian placenta has compartmentalized into more complex cellular domains.
claims.source: However, we find that the tammar yolk sac placenta expresses many key markers of eutherian placental cell types, including those of maternal decidua. This suggests that the tammar yolk sac placenta perform functions that the eutherian placenta has compartmentalized into more complex cellular domains.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing expression of both maternal and fetal markers in the tammar placenta.

claims.claim: Global gene expression undergoes dynamic shifts from day 21 and 23 to day 25 during tammar gestation.
claims.source: Additionally we find that global gene expression undergoes dynamic shifts from day 21 and 23 to day 25, during tammar gestation, a window critical for placental growth and proliferation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Dynamic change in placental gene expression has been documented in the mouse and human.
claims.source: This same type of dynamic change in placental gene expression has also been documented in the mouse (Knox and Baker, 2008) and human (Winn et al., 2007) suggesting rapidly changing gene expression patterns may be conserved between therian placentas.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knox and Baker, 2008 and Winn et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Rapidly changing gene expression patterns may be conserved between therian placentas.
claims.source: This same type of dynamic change in placental gene expression has also been documented in the mouse (Knox and Baker, 2008) and human (Winn et al., 2007) suggesting rapidly changing gene expression patterns may be conserved between therian placentas.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of dynamic gene expression in tammar, mouse, and human placentas.

claims.claim: Many molecular functions of the placenta may be conserved in the therian mammal stem species.
claims.source: The presence and expression of core placental genes and the dynamic gene expression in the tammar placenta suggests that many molecular functions of the placenta may be conserved in the therian mammal stem species, as suggested previously (Freyer et al., 2002, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing conserved gene expression and supported by citations to Freyer et al., 2002, 2007.

claims.claim: The use of the placenta to distinguish eutherians from marsupials is incorrect.
claims.source: Furthermore, this strongly suggests that the use of the placenta to distinguish eutherians from marsupials is incorrect.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that marsupials have functional placentas with conserved molecular programs.

claims.claim: Reproductive genes have been shared between the placenta and the mammary gland throughout evolution to establish diverse lactation and placentation strategies.
claims.source: We suggest that reproductive genes have been shared between the placenta and the mammary gland throughout evolution to establish diverse lactation and placentation strategies to nourish mammalian young.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparative transcriptome analysis showing shared genes between placenta and mammary gland.

claims.claim: Genes shared between placenta and mammary gland are enriched for processes involved in nutrition, immune function and embryonic morphogenesis.
claims.source: The genes shared between these tissues are enriched for processes involved in nutrition, immune function and embryonic morphogenesis suggesting a functional convergence between placentation and lactation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claims.claim: There is functional convergence between placentation and lactation.
claims.source: The genes shared between these tissues are enriched for processes involved in nutrition, immune function and embryonic morphogenesis suggesting a functional convergence between placentation and lactation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the gene ontology analysis showing shared functional categories.

claims.claim: The mammary gland of the tammar shares the expression of transcripts that promote placental functions in eutherians, suggesting marsupial lactation is an alternate strategy that parallels eutherian placentation.
claims.source: Our finding that the mammary gland of the tammar shares the expression of transcripts, including Gcm1 (Anson-Cartwright et al., 2000) and Gata3 (Chiu and Chen, 2016), that promote placental functions in eutherians suggests marsupial lactation is an alternate strategy that parallels eutherian placentation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparative transcriptome analysis and immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Reproductive genes that allow efficient exchange between mother and offspring have been respectively co-opted in placentation and lactation to facilitate proper offspring growth and development.
claims.source: Taken together these data support the idea that reproductive genes that allow efficient exchange between mother and offspring have been respectively co-opted in placentation and lactation to facilitate proper offspring growth and development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparative transcriptome analysis showing shared genes between placenta and mammary gland.

claims.claim: BOM, with its large trophoblast layer, has a high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio allowing for greater uptake and subsequent metabolism of nutrients from uterine secretions.
claims.source: Many of the genes up-regulated in BOM fall into ontologies that are associated with nutrient uptake and metabolism. This is consistent with the hypothesis that BOM, with its large trophoblast layer, has a high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio allowing for greater uptake and subsequent metabolism of nutrients from uterine secretions (Renfree, 1973b; Renfree and Renfree, 1973a; Renfree and Tyndale-Biscoe, 1973; Freyer et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology data and citations.

claims.claim: TOM, having vasculature and a thin trophoblast layer, allows for rapid transport of oxygen thus acting as the primary site of embryonic respiration.
claims.source: Many of the genes up-regulated in TOM fall into ontologies that are associated with respiration. This is consistent with the idea that TOM, having vasculature and a thin trophoblast layer, allows for rapid transport of oxygen thus acting as the primary site of embryonic respiration (Renfree, 1973b; Renfree and Renfree, 1973a; Renfree and Tyndale-Biscoe, 1973; Freyer et al., 2002).

results.result: BOM and TOM tissues of the tammar placenta have distinct molecular profiles and functions. 445 transcripts were differentially expressed between BOM and TOM, with BOM enriched for genes related to endocytosis and metabolism (nutrient uptake), while TOM was enriched for genes related to extracellular matrix organization, hematopoiesis, and oxygen response (respiration).
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C41 are supported by DESeq2 differential expression analysis (Figure 2A) and gene ontology analysis with reported p-values. The functional interpretation is consistent with prior anatomical knowledge (Renfree, 1973b) and morphological observations (Freyer et al., 2002). The data demonstrate clear molecular specialization of the two placental tissue types.

results.result: The tammar placenta undergoes dynamic temporal changes in gene expression during late gestation. 1705 transcripts were differentially expressed between early (days 21-23) and late (day 25) time points, with late time points enriched for genes involved in cellular growth, differentiation, and junction organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by DESeq2 analysis (Figure 2B) and gene ontology analysis with reported p-values. The temporal dynamics are consistent with the critical window of TOM expansion and placental maturation. The finding parallels documented dynamic expression in mouse and human placentas.

results.result: The tammar placenta shares expression of 3894 core placental genes with mouse and human placentas, including key trophoblast markers (Gcm1, Igf pathway genes, cytokeratins, Wnt7b, Cdx2), maternal decidual markers (Cebpb, Vim), and factors mediating maternal-fetal interactions (cathepsins, serpins).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C55 are supported by comparative transcriptome analysis across three species. Each marker is validated by appropriate citations. The finding of shared core genes despite morphological differences provides strong evidence for molecular conservation in placental function across therian mammals.

results.result: Immunofluorescence reveals unexpected protein localization patterns in the tammar placenta: maternal decidual markers (CEBPB, Vimentin) are expressed in both endodermal and trophoblast layers, while eutherian trophoblast markers (Pan-Cytokeratins, GCM1) are expressed only in the endodermal layer, suggesting functional compartmentalization differs from eutherians.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 3) showing clear layer-specific and pan-layer expression patterns. The findings are surprising given established eutherian marker distributions (supported by citations C61-C62) and suggest the tammar placenta has accomplished functional coordination differently than eutherians. However, the interpretation (C64) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The tammar placenta transcriptome most closely resembles early mouse placentation (e10.5), with significant enrichment for early placental transcripts (90/340 early vs 10/70 late mouse placental genes, p<0.05 by chi-square test).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by Spearman correlation analysis (Figure 4A) and enrichment analysis with appropriate statistical testing. The use of mouse heart as a control (C69) strengthens the conclusion that the similarity is placenta-specific. The chi-square test (C73) provides statistical support for the enrichment of early transcripts.

results.result: Cross-species organ comparisons reveal that tammar and mouse placentas share the highest correlation of any cross-species organ pair, while mammary glands show lower but significant conservation. GATA3, a transcription factor essential for mouse placentation, is expressed in tammar mammary gland alveoli in a pattern reminiscent of mouse mammary gland expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are supported by Spearman correlation analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 5B). The GATA3 expression pattern supports an ancestral role in lactation (C82), though this is somewhat inferential. The low within-species correlation between placenta and mammary gland (C83) appropriately suggests divergent organ functions.

results.result: 77 genes are shared between tammar placenta, eutherian placenta, and tammar mammary gland (but not mouse mammary gland), enriched for nutrient transport functions (p-adj=0.0163). This includes GCM1, which shows strong nuclear expression in tammar mammary gland alveoli, suggesting convergent co-option of placental genes by the marsupial mammary gland.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 are supported by comparative transcriptome analysis (Figure 5A), gene ontology analysis with reported p-value, and immunofluorescence data (Figure 5B). The interpretation of convergent co-option (C91) is somewhat speculative but reasonable given the data. The control comparisons with liver and testis strengthen the specificity of the finding.

results.result: 108 genes are shared between eutherian placenta and tammar mammary gland (but not tammar placenta and mouse mammary gland), trending toward embryonic morphogenesis and immune function (p-adj=0.163, 0.146). These include genes with documented placental roles (Dkk1, Csf1r, Igfbp1), suggesting the tammar mammary gland performs functions similar to late eutherian placenta.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by comparative transcriptome analysis (Figure 5A), but the gene ontology analysis did not reach statistical significance (C93), only showing trends. While specific genes with placental roles are identified (C94-C95), the overall functional interpretation (C96) is somewhat speculative given the lack of significant GO enrichment. Control comparisons were performed but also lacked significant enrichment.

results.result: The tammar yolk sac placenta expresses markers of both maternal and fetal eutherian placental cell types and undergoes dynamic gene expression changes during gestation, suggesting molecular functions are conserved in the therian stem species and that using placentation to distinguish eutherians from marsupials is incorrect.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by the immunofluorescence data (C97), temporal differential expression analysis (C98), and citations to similar dynamics in mouse and human (C99). The inference of conservation in the therian stem species (C101) and the conclusion about nomenclature (C102) are reasonable given the totality of evidence, though somewhat interpretive.

results.result: Reproductive genes have been shared between placenta and mammary gland throughout mammalian evolution, with genes enriched for nutrition, immune function, and embryonic morphogenesis, suggesting functional convergence between placentation and lactation as alternate strategies for offspring support.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by the comparative transcriptome analysis and gene ontology data (C104). The interpretation of functional convergence (C105) and evolutionary co-option (C103, C107) is inferential but well-supported by the molecular data showing shared gene expression between organs with similar developmental support functions. The finding that tammar mammary gland expresses placental transcription factors (C106) strengthens this interpretation.

results.result: BOM's large trophoblast layer with high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio facilitates nutrient uptake and metabolism, while TOM's vasculature and thin trophoblast layer enable rapid oxygen transport for embryonic respiration. The trophoblast thinning in TOM parallels convergent thinning of maternal-fetal interhemal distance in eutherian placentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by gene ontology data consistent with these functions and multiple citations to prior anatomical work (Renfree, 1973b; Freyer et al., 2002). The observation of morphological convergence (C110) is supported by citation to Enders and Carter, 2004, though the interpretation is somewhat inferential.

results.result: The endodermal layer of the tammar placenta expresses GCM1 and Pan-cytokeratins (eutherian trophoblast markers), suggesting it serves as the center of nutrient trafficking. The trophoblast layer expresses CEBPB and Vimentin (eutherian decidual markers), suggesting the two layers play roles analogous to eutherian trophoblast and decidua, respectively, despite the absence of decidualization in tammar.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing layer-specific expression patterns and appropriate citations for marker functions in eutherians. The interpretation that layers have analogous roles (C117) is inferential but reasonable given the expression data. The absence of decidualization in tammar (C115) is established knowledge, making the expression of decidual markers particularly noteworthy.

results.result: Despite anatomical simplicity, the tammar placenta expresses a dynamic molecular program highly reminiscent of eutherian placentation, with sub-functionalization of cell layers to express both maternal and fetal placental genes. This demonstrates molecular conservation in mammalian placentation despite morphological variation and suggests genes can move between cell types during evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are summary conclusions supported by the totality of transcriptome and immunofluorescence data presented. The molecular conservation (C122) is well-demonstrated, and the sub-functionalization (C120) is supported by the layer-specific expression data. The evolutionary interpretation about gene mobility (C119, C121) is more speculative but reasonable given the evidence.

results.result: Marsupials have placentas to mediate embryonic development and more complex milk repertoires than eutherians. Dynamic lactation evolved in marsupials as an alternative to complex eutherian placentation, with marsupials relying more heavily on lactation for fetal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10, and C33 are supported by citations to established literature and the data presented in the manuscript. These represent accepted knowledge in the field that provides context for the study's findings.

results.result: Background information on placental function, morphology, and development in various mammalian species, including tammar wallaby anatomy, pregnancy/lactation durations, milk composition, and cellular composition of eutherian vs marsupial placentas.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C32, C42, C56-C57, C65-C67, C75-C76 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide essential background context for interpreting the new findings but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that the anatomically simple tammar placenta expresses a dynamic molecular program reminiscent of eutherian placentation and provides evidence for convergent co-option of genes by placental and mammary gland cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 are the primary stated findings of the abstract, supported by the comprehensive transcriptome and immunofluorescence data presented throughout the Results section. These represent the main conclusions of the manuscript.
